title: Why Is Ice Slippery?
subject: Physics
objective: Not because your weight melts it: that lowers the melting point by only a fraction of a degree. A thin liquid-like surface layer (premelting) and frictional melting do the work, and scientists still debate the details.

fill.q: The old idea that our weight melts ice is called ____ melting.
A liquid-like layer on ice below 0 °C is called ____.
The premelting layer was first proposed by Michael ____.

tf.q: Pressure from our weight lowers the melting point of ice by several degrees.
tf.explain: Only by a fraction of a degree.

tf.q: Ice can be slippery even at −30 °C.
A moving skate can melt a thin water film by friction.
Scientists fully agree on why ice is slippery.

ar.a: Ice is slippery even when you stand still.
ar.r: A liquid-like layer covers ice below 0 °C.
Pressure lowers the melting point of ice.
ar.explain: A is false (the effect is a fraction of a degree); R is true.

mcq.q: Why does pressure melting fail as the full explanation?
options: the melting point falls only a fraction of a degree
mcq.explain: The effect is far too small.
A thin mobile layer exists below the melting point.

num.q: Pressure lowers ice's melting point by about 0.0074 °C per atmosphere. By how much does a pressure of 100 atmospheres lower it?
num.answer: about 0.74 °C, far too little to explain slipping at −30 °C

short.q: Explain the three ideas proposed for why ice is slippery.
short.solution: Pressure melting: weight melts the ice (too small an effect). Frictional melting: sliding heats and melts a thin film (true for moving skates). Premelting: a liquid-like layer exists on ice below 0 °C (explains slipping even when standing still).

short.q: Why is this called an open question?
short.solution: Experiments confirm a mobile surface layer and frictional melting, but how much each contributes, and the exact behaviour of the surface molecules, is still being researched.

right: Melts a film under a moving skate
match.explain: Each idea matches its role in the explanation.
